list.listitem: A group of symptoms that happen traditionally following high carbohydrate diet consumption or with undigested food rapidly reaching the small intestine from altered gastric anatomy and innervation after certain upper gastrointestinal (GI) surgeries, most commonly after bariatric surgery. C

Early dumping syndrome can present with GI symptoms (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, bloating, belching, diarrhea) or vasomotor symptoms (dizziness, palpitations, flushing, fatigue, and desire to lay down) occurring within 1 hour after eating, but usually within the first 30 minutes. C
Late dumping can present sweating, dizziness, lightheadedness, weakness, shakiness, palpitations, diarrhea, fainting, mental confusion, and hypoglycemia occurring 1 to 3 hours after eating. C

Dumping may improve with dietary modification including frequent small meals low in carbohydrates and high in protein, fiber, avoiding fluids 15 min before and until 30 minutes after the meal, or addition of pectin or guar gum. B
Dumping occasionally requires medications like acarbose, octreotide or verapamil; B rarely, surgical revision is needed. C

background.definition: A constellation of symptoms that occur when undigested osmotically active food is dumped into the small intestine too rapidly. Often post upper GI surgery, but may be due to vagus nerve damage. Symptoms can be divided into early (more common) and late dumping syndrome based on timing. The latter results primarily from a hyperinsulinemic response to carbohydrate ingestion.

list.listitem: Variable: up to 75% of patients dumped following gastric bypass surgery, less in sleeve gastrectomy surgery; among these patients 10% to 15% had severe symptoms.
In another study of 1,153 post-gastrectomy patients, the incidences of early or late dumping syndrome were 67.6% and 38.4%, respectively.

Following laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy, dumping syndrome occurs early postoperatively (as measured by provocation test) in 45% of patients. In one small follow-up study of 25 patients, symptoms suggestive of dumping syndrome were found in 40% of patients at 6 months and in 33% at 12 months postoperatively.

In a larger follow-up study of 440 patients post sleeve gastrectomy or primary Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, early dumping was suspected in 9.1% and 19.4%, respectively and late dumping in 6.7% and 11.4%, respectively.

Dumping was seen in up to 14% of patients initially after truncal vagotomy with drainage procedure but dropped to 4% seven years after surgery. There was a 20% incidence after partial gastrectomy and 1% to 2% after highly selective vagotomy.
The presence of dumping appears to improve weight loss following Roux-en-Y gastric bypass.

In a Swedish follow-up study of 188 esophageal cancer survivors one year after surgery, moderate early dumping was present in 45% and severe in 9%; moderate late dumping was reported by 13% and severe late dumping in 5%. Health-related quality of life (HRQOL) was poorer for those reporting severe early dumping in 4 of 7 aspects with clinically large differences in global QOL and social function compared to those having no dumping symptoms. Similarly, patients with moderate late dumping symptoms reported poorer HRQL in 6 out of 7 aspects and those with severe symptoms had clinically large declines in cognitive and emotional function compared to those with no dumping symptoms.
Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery.
Gastrojejunostomy.
Sleeve gastrectomy surgery.
Vagotomy.
Pyloroplasty.
Nissen fundoplication.
Nonsurgical causes include diabetes mellitus, viral illness, and idiopathic.

Early dumping (within 1 hour of eating) occurs as a result of rapid emptying of hypertonic liquids into the small bowel. It is usually described following a high-carbohydrate meal but can occur after high fat consumption.
Late dumping (1-3 hour after eating) occurs from rapid absorption of glucose, resulting in hyperinsulinemia.
The change in gastric anatomy and innervation resulting from various gastric surgeries affect gastric emptying and cause these dumping conditions.

Recent data suggest that increased production of gut hormones such as glucagon-like peptide (GLP)-1, pancreatic polypeptide, peptide YY, enteroglucagon, and neurotensin play a role in gastrointestinal motility and cause dumping symptoms. In a case series of 40 patients who underwent gastrectomy for gastric cancer, there were greater postprandial increases in blood glucose, GLP-1 and GLP-2 levels, and heart rate among gastrectomy patients compared to controls and greater increases in these parameters for patients undergoing total gastrectomy vs. distal gastrectomy. In one small study, administration of a GLP-1r receptor antagonist prevented hypoglycemia and reversed neuroglycopenic symptoms.

Vasomotor symptoms are influenced by vasoactive intestinal peptide and serotonin; the former causing increased bowel contractions, dilation of intestinal blood vessels, and secretion of water and electrolytes into the intestinal lumen. Bradykinin also appears to have a role in post-surgical vasomotor symptoms.

It is hypothesized that the hormonally-mediated fluid shift from the general circulation to the intestinal lumen and intestinal blood supply is so dramatic in dumping syndrome that compensatory mechanisms are overwhelmed causing symptoms such as weakness, fatigue, dyspnea, and hypotension, if severe.
Select surgeries that have a low incidence of dumping syndromes, namely proximal vagotomy instead of truncal vagotomy for ulcer treatment. C

Use of pylorus-preserving gastrectomy vs. conventional distal gastrectomy for early middle-third gastric cancer is associated with less early dumping (Odds Ratio (OR) 0.18; 95% CI 0.12-0.27), based on a series of nonrandomized clinical trials.

In meta-analysis of 17 RCTs and 8 observational studies including 1621 patients undergoing total gastrectomy, the creation of a pouch (small bowel reservoir) markedly reduced the risk of dumping syndrome at 3 to 6 months (8.1% vs 32.4%; Risk Ratio [RR] 0.36, 95% CI 0.21-0.60) and 12 to 24 months (2.8% vs 23.6%; RR 0.27, 95% CI 0.16-0.46). There was no difference in post-operative complications.

In a meta-analysis of 10 studies of patients undergoing total gastrostomy, jejunal interposition reconstruction rather than Roux-en-Y anastomosis had a lower risk of dumping syndrome (OR 0.18; 95% CI 0.10-0.31) as well as other complications and was associated with improved quality of life.

In a case series of 157 patients undergoing Roux-en-y reconstruction after laparoscopy-assisted distal gastrectomy for gastric carcinoma, preservation of the celiac branch of the vagus nerve was associated with less dumping at 12 months postoperatively (2 patients [2.9%] vs. 14 patients [15.7%]). C

In the large case series noted above, factors associated with reduced risk of early dumping included reduced weight loss, old age, pylorus preserving gastrectomy, distal gastrectomy with Roux-Y reconstruction, and distal gastrectomy with Billroth I. Factors associated with a decreased risk of late dumping were reduced weight loss, being male, pylorus preserving gastrectomy, and distal gastrectomy with Roux-Y reconstruction. C

In a follow-up study of patients undergoing laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass with or without transection of the lesser omentum for morbid obesity, patients without lesser omental transection reported significantly fewer symptoms (including dumping). The authors postulated that this may be due to inadvertent partial vagotomy that can occur if the lesser omentum is transected. C
Alcohol, such as drinking a glass of wine with meals, may slow gastric emptying and reduce early dumping through its augmented anticholinergic effect in the setting of vagal nerve denervation.

Dumping syndrome is diagnosed clinically based on typical symptoms recurring after eating (eg, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, cramps, bloating, belching, diarrhea, dizziness, palpitations, flushing, fatigue, and confusion) in a patient with history of gastric surgery. C

The diagnosis can be confirmed with a glucose challenge test. The test is not usually necessary unless there is a clinical uncertainty or a need to confirm the diagnosis prior to surgical management. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Abdominal pain, distention, nausea, vomiting, hyperactive bowel sounds initially
Abdominal cramps, diarrhea associated with eating, nutrient deficiencies, weight loss
Flushing, diarrhea, abdominal cramps, heart valve lesions
Abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, fever, rectal bleeding

list.listitem: Suspect early dumping syndrome in patients with a history of gastric surgery and nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, cramps, bloating, belching, diarrhea, dizziness, palpitations, flushing, fatigue, and desire to lie down within 1 hour of meals.

Suspect late dumping syndrome in patients with a history of gastric surgery and sweating, dizziness, lightheadedness, fatigue, weakness, shakiness, palpitations, diarrhea, fainting, mental confusion, or hypoglycemia 1 to 3 hours after meals. Symptoms occur especially following a high carbohydrate meal (sucrose and fructose).
Typical recurrence of dumping symptoms is followed by ingestion of high carbohydrate food.
Rise in pulse rate, drop in blood pressure, pallor, sweating, and general distress can be found on examination during the episode.

In one study of 70 patients with suspected rapid gastric emptying (RGE) and 572 with presumed gastroparesis, gastrointestinal symptoms had poor specificity for the actual rate of gastric emptying on scintigraphy. Among patients with RGE, the PV+ of clinical suspicion for RGE was 62%; 79% of patients with rapid emptying on scintigraphy had no obvious explanation for this result.

Dumping syndrome is primarily a clinical diagnosis. Consider testing in patients with clinical uncertainty for confirmation of symptoms that could be coming from other conditions like gastroparesis or for diagnostic confirmation before attempting surgical correction.

The preferred test is a provocation test using a 50% hypertonic glucose solution; patients with dumping syndrome will have a greater fall in plasma volume and steeper rises in blood sugar after ingestion of the solution.

A panel of international experts in dumping syndrome recommend a protocol of ingestion of 75 g of glucose in solution after an overnight fast with measurement of blood concentrations of glucose, hematocrit level, pulse rate and blood pressure before and at 30-min intervals up to 180 min after ingestion. A positive test for early dumping is an increase in hematocrit level >3% or an increase in pulse rate of >10 beats per minute 30 minutes after ingestion.
An increase of 10 or more beats per minute in heart rate was 100% sensitive and 94% specific for early dumping in one small study of postoperative patients.

An additional finding after the glucose challenge test is initial hyperglycemia and late hypoglycemia (<60 mg/dL). The panel of international experts had higher agreement with using a lower level of glucose of <50 mg/dL as indicative of late dumping.

Gastric emptying studies may be helpful in difficult cases. One such test, the 13C-Spirulina platensis breath test, measures gastric emptying t1/2 for solids. In one study of healthy patients given drugs to simulate dumping, sensitivity was 86% and specificity 80% for abnormal emptying. Gastric emptying was significantly faster and fall in plasma volume significantly greater in patients who experienced symptoms after the ingestion of hypertonic glucose than who did not. The panel of experts concluded that gastric emptying tests had low utility for diagnosing dumping syndrome based on low sensitivity and specificity.
Another option is the hydrogen breath test; an early rise in breath H2 excretion in one study had a sensitivity or 84% and specificity of 94% for early dumping.
Endoscopy should be done to rule out other causes or anatomical problems if clinically suspected.

A clinical diagnostic index was described by Sigstad on dumping syndrome to be used as a diagnostic aid. The panel of international experts in dumping syndrome, however, did not reach consensus on the value of either Sigstad’s questionnaire or Art’s dumping questionnaire for either identifying patients with dumping syndrome or monitoring therapy.

Suspect dumping syndrome in patients with typical symptoms after gastric surgery; signs and symptoms of hypovolemia occur in early dumping syndrome, and those of hypoglycemia occur in late dumping syndrome.
Confirmatory testing using a 50% hypertonic glucose solution should be considered in patients with clinical uncertainty or for diagnostic confirmation before attempting surgical correction.

Patients usually benefit from dietary modification with small frequent meals, avoiding simple carbohydrates, increasing protein and fiber content in meals, avoiding fluids with meals and until 30 min after meals, and adding pectin and/or guar gum. Symptoms usually improve over time. Consider a medication trial if diet modification does not help. B
Acarbose can improve late dumping. B
Octreotide can improve symptoms in the short term for early and late dumping. B

Surgical revision has been considered in severe or persistent cases of hypoglycemia when gastric remnant feeds improved dumping symptoms, even though recent studies demonstrate variable outcomes with recurrence of symptoms. C

Acarbose (50-100 mg 3 times daily 15 minutes before meals) can improve symptoms in late dumping syndrome; 100% success was seen in one small study. This occurs by inhibiting the release of GLP1 secretion. The panel of international experts endorse use of acarbose for symptoms of late dumping.
Verapamil and acarbose combined may be helpful in some patients.
In a case report, diazoxide was helpful for reducing postprandial hypoglycemia in a child with late dumping syndrome following transplant surgery.

The panel of international experts endorse use of somatostatin analogues, particularly short-acting formulations, for patients with well-established dumping syndrome who do not respond to diet changes with or without acarbose.

Octreotide,an octapeptide that mimics somatostatin, can provide initial relief and can be used in both early and late dumping; evidence for long-term efficacy is limited. Octreotide is given as 25 to 50 mg subcutaneously up to 3 times daily, one-half hour before meals. Octreotide depot suspension (Sandostatin LAR) is given as 10 to 20 mg intramuscularly every 4 weeks for 6 months. In one study, octreotide (25-200 mg/d) provided sustained relief in 80% of patients (mean follow-up 37 ± 9 months).

In a phase II trial of lanreotide, a long-acting somatostatin analogue, improvement in early but not late dumping syndrome was reported although side effects were common, including 7 serious adverse events among the 24 patients in the study.

Side effects of somatostatin analogues include steatorrhea, diarrhea, nausea, gallstone formation, pain at injection site and weight gain. Authors of one review recommend starting at low doses (25 mg octreotide) and titrating up to a maximum of 100 mg and discontinuing the drug after 2 weeks (subcutaneous) or 2 months (intramuscular) if there is no improvement.

In a phase 2 study of 43 patients with late dumping of whom 33 finished the 3-month trial, subcuticular pasireotide, a long-acting cyclic hexapeptide with somatostatin-like activity, reduced hypoglycemia to 60% of patients and improved quality of life. Headache was the most common side effect occurring in 34.9%.
Case reports support the use of subcuticular liraglutide or oral sitagliptin, a dipeptidyl-peptidase 4 inhibitor (50 mg/day), to reduce postprandial hypoglycemia after gastric surgery.
Studies are also underway on an inhibitor of calcium-activated chloride channel transmembrane member16A, one determinant of gastric motility.
Good results have been shown from conversion of gastric surgeries that are causing symptoms.

Results were excellent with gastrojejunal stoma revision and conversion of Billroth II (gastrojejunal anastomosis) to Billroth I (gastroduodenal anastomosis) in one study was 92% successful. In a retrospective case series of 40 patients with dumping syndrome undergoing endoscopic gastro-jejunal revision for a dilated gastro-jejunal anastomosis following Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, most (33/37), treated only endoscopically, had improved or resolved symptoms during the minimum 1-month follow-up period.

Jejunal interposition was also found to be highly successful based on multiple studies, and pyloric reconstruction and conversion to Roux-en-Y gastrojejunostomy have been tried in severe cases with positive outcomes.
No randomized controlled studies comparing surgeries has been done.
Pectin and guar gum use is controversial. Some studies showed delayed gastric emptying and improvement in symptoms with pectin, but no change was found in a later study.
In several studies, a semi solid meal containing 5 g of guar gum was useful in slowing gastric emptying in 5 of 11 patients with dumping. However, these agents can cause bloating and gas.
It is unclear if herbal medicine is effective for dumping syndrome.
Hypnotherapy has been tried with 63% good or excellent symptomatic relief in one study.

Initial treatment typically includes dietary changes, although clinical trials are lacking. Recommend small frequent meals containing low carbohydrates, high protein, and the addition of pectin or guar gum (as described above).
Consumption of liquids should occur between meals rather than with them.

In a study of 10 patients following Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, sitting vs. supine position and high volume (150 ml) vs. low volume (50 ml) drinks was associated with more rapid pouch emptying and increased gastrointestinal symptoms suggesting a role for not sitting when eating and lower volume liquids. Protein pre-load may also be useful.
Nutritional manipulation alone, using a combination of complex carbohydrate and a fat emulsion, completely resolved symptoms in children who developed dumping symptoms after fundoplication surgery.
Uncooked cornstarch also controlled symptoms in pediatric populations.
Jejunostomy feeding tube can be considered in malnourished patients with inadequate oral intake.

In a small case series of 29 of 97 patients who underwent esophagogastrectomy and had delayed gastric emptying resistant to systemic pharmacological treatment, 1 to 2 treatments of endoscopically administered Botulinum toxin into the pylorus was successful in all patients.
Consider referral for treatment when patient has severe symptoms and to rule out other causes.
Prognosis is good; approximately two-thirds of patient's symptoms will completely resolve in time and one-sixth will partially improve based on one long-term study. B
In a 3-year follow-up study of patients following Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, the prevalence of dumping at least once weekly decreased from 9.9% to 6.3% at year 3.
